_comment: The planet editor's parameter catalogue (plan §5.1, §7.12 setup page): one list for the game's Create World editor (screen/model/EditorFields reads it from the jar as deeptime/editor_fields.json; Gradle copies it like ramps.json) and the browser workbench (deeptime watch, P1-20). Each field names the preset JSON path it edits (dots; a number in a path is an array index, e.g. structure.pluton_length_km.0); a field is editable exactly when the selected preset carries that path, so neither side adds keys a preset does not know. Labels are the lang keys deeptime.editor.field.<id> and deeptime.editor.section.<section> (neoforge/src/main/resources/assets/deeptime/lang/en_us.json), and for a choice deeptime.editor.option.<id>.<value>. kind: number | toggle | choice (a choice lists its options); planned marks a setting whose stage or preset key does not exist yet (canyons arrive with Phase 2; the pack-defined essentials lists with the datapack loader): it shows as not in the preset and the built-ins need not carry it (ModelHelpersTest.realPresetsCarryEveryField); an optional stops list names values worth one click (the workbench shows them as buttons; the game puts them in the hint); integer numbers are written as JSON integers (the seed is a u64), other numbers as doubles; phase3 marks a fantasy toggle shown disabled until Phase 3. The planet, scale and seed paths and ranges are P1-03's params.rs (PlanetParams, ScaleParams, PlanetPreset::validate); the sections `terrain` and `adv_*` (settings audit, decisions log 2026-09-29: tuning knobs that shape the world are settings, not constants) name keys the pipeline presets carry at their calibrated values, so a default run is unchanged; their ranges were run at both ends on a small planet (STATUS.md, build log settings audit); where two fields can contradict each other the core refuses the pair with a message that names the fields (planet.ocean_fraction with the flooded margin: no ocean floor left). The remaining fields are proposals for stages that have not landed (the core validates in the end). hint is a one-line description of a field and sections a one-line description of each section: the workbench shows both under the controls and the game shows the hint as a tooltip. advanced_sections lists the sections both editors keep collapsed until asked for (the game groups them under one Advanced header). Left out because the model does not read them: tectonics.abyssal_elevation_m and trench_elevation_m (validated, never used). Left out on purpose (deposits.max_formed_per_survivor, a cap on the count model; internal numerics and calibration constants, not choices about the world): iteration counts, solver tolerances, tile and grid sizes, time steps, frame and snapshot intervals, layer counts, event-detection thresholds, the energy-balance model's radiation constants, the orographic-rain physics constants and the plate model's Cortial constants other than those listed.

sections.planet: The world itself: its seed, gravity, day, tilt, sunlight and oceans.
sections.scale: How much real planet one block stands for, across and up.
sections.terrain: How the land looks: how steep the slopes are, how deeply rivers carve them, how rugged mountains are, how glaciers shape them, how many volcanoes stand on it and how often meteors strike it.
sections.multipliers: Scale deposits and terrain features up or down, relative to the preset.
sections.biomes: Where the pack's biomes go on the simulated climate: shifts, beaches, patch sizes, swamps.
sections.fantasy: Terrain beyond geology. It arrives in Phase 3, so these stay off for now.
sections.playability: Guarantees that make a world playable, whatever its history.
sections.adv_plates: How many plates and continents the planet starts with, how deep its oceans are and how fast mountains and island arcs are built.
sections.adv_surface: How fast rivers, hillslopes and waves wear the land down, how the crust rebounds, and how the sea rises and falls.
sections.adv_climate: Temperature, rain and ice: how the climate treats the land, and the greenhouse, sunlight and ice ages over deep time.
sections.adv_rocks: The granite bodies that intrude under mountain belts, how rock layers run from place to place, and the folds and faults that deform them.
sections.adv_volcanoes: Where volcanoes form along arcs and over hotspots, how big they grow, when they collapse into calderas and how they age.
sections.adv_impacts: Meteor impacts: how the sizes of craters are spread, how fast and dense the impactors are, how far ejecta reach, how deep a sea stops an impactor and how quickly craters fade.
sections.adv_deposits: How ore deposits cluster into regions.
sections.adv_biomes: How far from the sea the inland biome bands begin, where swamps may form, and how big the geologic provinces are that biome-mod regions (TerraBlender) follow.
sections.adv_water: Rivers and lakes: how many streams there are, how wide and deep their channels, how lakes fill and where river biomes go.
sections.adv_underground: Where lava is: the magma under active volcanoes and their crater lakes, the lava at the bottom of the world, and whether biomes scatter lava lakes of their own.
sections.adv_geothermal: Hot springs, terraces, fumaroles and altered ground around the active volcanoes: how many, how far from the summit, how big, and how much rain a field needs to be hot springs rather than steam vents. The pools are plain water: there are no geysers, steam or boiling.

fields.hint: Seeds the whole history: the same seed and settings make closely similar planets, but identical worlds are not guaranteed between machines or versions.
Surface gravity. Earth: 9.81 m/s².
Hours from one sunrise to the next (a solar day); the planet's spin is worked out from it. Earth: 24 h.
Tilt of the spin axis, which sets the seasons and climate belts. Earth: 23.4°.
Sunlight reaching the planet, relative to Earth's.

Share of the surface under the sea. Earth: about 0.71 (the built-in presets use 0.7). Continental crust may fill at most 98 % of the crust, so this must stay above 1 − 0.98 × (1 − the flooded continental margin): about 0.30 at the default margin of 0.29 (the slider stops at 0.31), more for a wider margin (0.61 at a margin of 0.6).
Metres of planet per block, east–west and north–south. Small values make a tiny planet whose rivers and waves wear it flat; the default is 300.
Metres of planet per block, up and down: smaller values make taller terrain. Below about 20 m the highest ranges no longer fit under the world's height limit and are squeezed into the band below.
Terrain that would stand above the world's height limit is squeezed smoothly into a band this thick under it instead of being cut flat. Everything below the band is as simulated. Default 48.
Steepness of slopes and the strength of fine terrain detail. 1 is as simulated.
How deeply rivers may cut valleys into the finished terrain, as a multiple of the local relief. Subtle 0.5, medium 3 (the default), dramatic 10 (practically no limit).

Rivers carved into the terrain along the simulated drainage, and lakes sized by the climate: a basin that gets more water than its surface evaporates fills to the brim and spills, a drier one holds a smaller lake, a salt flat or nothing, and a cold one is frozen over. Off leaves no water above sea level.
How hard glaciers grind their beds, relative to Earth's glaciers: they carve troughs and fjords, plane mountains down towards the snowline and leave till. 0 lets ice sit without eroding.

How wide the valleys the last ice ages carved are drawn, as a multiple of a real glacier's width. At the game's scale a real glacial valley is only a few blocks wide and looks like a gorge; 3 (the default) makes U-shaped valleys read as U-shaped. The planet's long history is not affected.
How far valleys the last ice ages filled are turned into U-shaped troughs with cirques at their heads, in the finished terrain. 1 is the shape a glacier wears its valley into.

Block-scale mountain character: ridges and gullies down the slopes along the simulated drainage, cliff bands on hard rock, sharp young peaks and rounded old ones. 0 leaves the simulated terrain smooth; 1 (the default) is the look the planets are tuned for.
How many volcanoes stand along volcanic arcs and hotspot tracks: it divides their spacing, so 2 packs them twice as close and 0 makes none (flood basalts still come from the plates).

How tall and wide volcanoes grow, and how big their calderas are, as a multiple of the default sizes (at 1 a stratovolcano stands 0.6–2 km high, where Earth's median is about 1 km, and a shield 3.5–6.5 km above the sea floor; Mauna Loa stands about 9 km above its sea floor).

How steep volcano flanks are, as a share of the real profile: heights are drawn 15 times larger than widths (a block is 300 m across and 20 m tall), so real proportions (1) make steep spires; the default 0.5 makes cones twice as broad at the same height.

How often meteors strike, as a multiple of Earth's recent rate: 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ craters of 20 km or more per km² per year, about one every 350,000 years over the whole Earth (estimated from craters younger than about 120 million years on stable continents). Most craters erode, are buried or go down with the sea floor, so few show at any time; 0 makes none.

How deep impact craters are, as a share of their real depth. At the default scale a block is 300 m across but 20 m high, so heights are drawn 15 times steeper than the ground is wide, so real proportions (1) make a small crater a shaft about three times deeper than wide; the default 0.5 halves every crater's depth, rim and central peak.
How many ore deposits form, relative to the preset.
How much ore each deposit holds, relative to real deposits: its body grows with it (twice the ore, a body 26 % wider each way). The number of deposits stays.
How rich the ore is, relative to real deposits: the share of metal in the ore. Grades cannot pass 100 %, so very high values saturate.
How strongly each ore type clusters into its own regions: off spreads them evenly, strong makes distinct ore provinces.

How big ore bodies are drawn in blocks (length, width and height), without changing how much ore they hold. 1 is the default drawing size, which already enlarges every deposit type to read at the block scale; real deposits are much smaller in blocks.
How wide rivers are drawn in blocks, for the same discharge. 1 is the default (a stream at the drawing threshold is a block wide, the largest rivers a few dozen); 2 doubles every channel.
Size of canyons in blocks.
How thick rock layers are drawn in blocks, without changing the history or the ore. 1 is the true thickness at the block scale; 2 makes every layer twice as thick.
How strongly rock is folded and how far faults offset it where plates collided, subducted or rifted. 0 leaves every layer as it was laid down, with no folds or faults.
How many folds and faults form where the crust is squeezed, stretched or sheared. Cratons stay flat whatever this is.

How much young faults and folds show on the ground: fault scarps, rift valleys between facing faults, ridges over fresh anticlines. 0 keeps them in the rock only. Old structures are worn flat whatever this is.
How many small intrusions cut the layers: granite stocks in mountain belts, basalt dykes along rifts, and the plugs of extinct volcanoes. 0 leaves only the large granite bodies.
Moves every biome warmer (+) or colder (−), in vanilla temperature bands. 0 follows the simulated climate.
Moves every land biome wetter (+) or drier (−), in vanilla humidity bands. 0 follows the simulated climate.
Width of the coast band on land, where beaches and stony shores go.
The window relief and ridges are measured over: the size of the patches of peak, slope, plateau and plains biomes.
Size of the patches of variant biomes (sunflower plains, ice spikes, bamboo jungle and the like).
How readily wet, flat lowlands become swamps and mangroves. 0 makes none.
Magical ore fields and landforms beyond geology.
Floating islands above the terrain.
Landforms no real planet makes.
The materials every region is guaranteed, from the pack's essentials list.
How many plates the crust starts in. More plates make smaller continents, more collisions and more rifts. Earth: about 14.
How many separate continents the scattered start begins with. The supercontinent start ignores it.
How often plates split apart along new rifts. 0 keeps every plate whole; the default is 0.012.
Depth of the mid-ocean ridge crests, the shallowest part of the sea floor. Earth: about −2,500 m.
Depth the ocean floor sinks to as it ages and cools away from the ridges: the abyssal plains. Earth: about −5,600 m. Must stay deeper than the ridges.
Share of the continental crust that lies under the sea as shelf and shallow sea. Earth: 0.29.
How fast volcanic island arcs build up above a subducting plate. Faster arcs reach the surface sooner and grow new continental crust.
How fast mountains rise on the edge of a continent where an ocean plate dives beneath it (Andes-style).
How far inland the mountain belt above a subduction zone reaches. The Andes: 400–900 km.
How far the uplift spreads when two continents collide (Himalaya-style). Larger values raise wide plateaus.
How fast a mountain range rises over a volcanic arc on a continent (Andes, Cascades), so its volcanoes stand on a range instead of a coastal plain. 0 leaves only the general subduction uplift.

How wide the range over a continental volcanic arc is. The setting is the distance from the arc's axis at which the uplift has fallen to 37 % (a gaussian scale), so the range is roughly twice this across (Earth-sized planet). The Cascades: about 100 km; the Central Andes: 300 km and more.
The height an arc range builds towards before its thickened crust spreads instead of rising. The Cascades' base: 1.2–2 km; the Andean plateau: about 4 km.

How much weight the crust carries before a range stops rising and spreads into a plateau. The plateau level is this divided by gravity: 140 MPa gives about 5 km at Earth's gravity (Tibet), about 13 km at Mars's. Summits stand a few kilometres above it.

How fast crust that stands above its strength spreads sideways. Higher values make flatter, wider plateaus closer to the strength level; 0 switches the spreading off, and ranges then rise until erosion alone stops them.
How readily old ocean floor breaks and starts sinking into a new subduction zone, which closes oceans (the end of a Wilson cycle). 0 keeps old ocean floor forever unless plates converge.
How old ocean floor must be before it can start sinking on its own. Earth's oldest ocean floor is about 180 million years old; passive margins last 180 million years on average.
How far from any working subduction zone old ocean floor must be to start a new one (Earth-sized planet).

How big a colliding continent must be, in average starting plates, to weld the two plates into one; it keeps the ocean on its other coasts, whose margins stay quiet. Smaller pieces are scraped off onto the other plate (island arcs, microcontinents).

How the model decides that two colliding continents have joined. On: when the crust between them has really shortened by the collision threshold (300 km), so plates that only slide past each other never join, and collisions last about 10 Myr instead of one step. Off (the default until collision mountain belts are built step by step): when speed times time since the continents first overlapped reaches the threshold, whichever way the plates move.

How much arc rock a volcanic island arc must build before its islands count as new continental crust. 0 turns every arc island into continent at once and continents grow fast; higher values grow them more slowly.

The overall speed of the plates under the force balance: a typical ocean plate pulled by a 3,000 km subduction zone moves at about this speed. Earth's plates move at a median of about 40 mm/yr. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How hard sinking slabs pull their plates, relative to the reference pull. Higher values make plates attached to subduction zones faster than the others. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How long a sinking slab grows before it pulls in full; a new subduction zone gains its pull as its slab lengthens. Earth's upper mantle is about 700 km deep. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How long continental crust must block a subduction zone before its slab tears off and stops pulling. Earth: about 10 to 25 Myr. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How strongly the mantle resists a slab's sinking, which sets the top speed of plates pulled by slabs. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How strongly a sinking slab draws the plate above it towards the trench, as a share of its pull. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How strongly high ground pushes plates: mid-ocean ridges push plates apart and high mountain belts push back against collisions. 0.1 is the strength the physics gives. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How much more the mantle drags on the deep roots of continents than on ocean floor. Earth: 2 to 5 times. Higher values make continents slower. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

How strongly plates resist sliding past and against each other along their edges. Higher values tie small plates to their neighbours. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.

The speed of a slow, broad flow of the mantle that drags plates no slab pulls, so that a planet with no subduction zones still moves. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.
How quickly a plate's motion follows the forces on it. Not active yet: the force balance is computed and recorded, but plates still move by the old speed rules until it is switched on.
How fast rivers cut into rock (the stream-power constant K). Higher values wear mountains down sooner and leave lower land; the default is 3e-9.

How much of the rock that erosion removes is made up again by the crust rising back. At 0.8 (about Earth) removing 1 km of rock lowers the ground by only 200 m; higher values keep mountains high for longer.

Whether the planet's outer shell is stiff. On: a mountain belt, a volcanic island or an ice sheet bends the crust around it, which makes basins in front of mountain ranges, moats round islands and a low rise beyond them. Off: every piece of ground sinks or rises on its own, as before this setting existed.

How thick the stiff part of the shell is, against Earth's (5 km under young mountains and volcanic arcs, 30 km under old ocean floor, 80 km under old continents). Stiffer shells make wider, shallower basins and hold narrow mountains higher. It only matters with plate bending on.
How fast soil creeps downhill and rounds hills off. Higher values give smoother, softer landscapes.
How strongly waves smooth shallow sea floors and wear coasts back. High values make coasts retreat and shelves wide.
Depth below which waves no longer move the sea floor.
How fast reefs and shallow warm seas build limestone. It sets how much limestone, dolostone and chalk a planet gets.
How fast salt and gypsum settle in hot, dry, cut-off seas.
Raises or lowers the sea for the whole history: positive floods the continents' edges, negative exposes more shelf.
Height of the slow sea-level cycle (period 250 Myr in the built-in presets) that floods and drains the continents' interiors. 0 keeps that cycle out.
How strongly ice sheets cool the planet by reflecting sunlight. 0 leaves the ice out of the heat balance; 1 is the full effect.
How fast the air cools with height. Earth: 6.5 °C per km. Steeper cooling puts snow lines lower.
How far sea air carries its moisture over land. Longer reach makes wetter continental interiors, shorter reach makes deserts.
How far the tropical rain belt swings north and south with the seasons over big continents. Larger swings mean stronger monsoons.
How much rain mountains wring from the wind, as hours of rain a day. Higher values give wetter windward slopes and drier lees.

How far below today's the snowline sat in the last ice ages, which shaped the youngest valleys. Earth's glacial average is about 500 m (the last glacial maximum about 900 m); 0 leaves only today's glaciers.
Share of the rock carved out of glacial troughs that goes back onto the ridges between them, keeping the mountains' mean height and sharpening their crests into arêtes and horns. 0 only carves.
Shifts the temperature at which glaciers can survive. Positive values let glaciers form in warmer places, negative values confine them to the cold.
Volcanoes breathe CO₂ out and rock weathering draws it down, so the greenhouse drifts with the plates. Off: CO₂ stays at the starting value.
CO₂ in the air at the start. 0 starts with volcanoes and weathering in balance; Earth before industry: 280 ppm.
How much CO₂ volcanoes and mountain belts release, against Earth's today for the same plate activity. Less makes a colder planet that can freeze over.
How readily warm, wet land weathers and draws CO₂ down. Stronger weathering makes a colder planet.
The star brightens as it ages, so the deep past gets less sunlight (about 4 % less 500 million years ago).

The star's age at the end of the history (the Sun: 4.57 billion years). The star is always at its present brightness at the end; a younger star was dimmer before that and brightens faster, so the deep past gets less sunlight.
How many million years at the end of the history get ice-age cycles from the wobbling orbit. 0: none.
How strongly the orbit wobbles in the ice-age window: tilt and eccentricity swings against Earth's.
How much ice sheets lower the sea by locking up water, exposing the shelves in ice ages. 0 leaves the sea level to its fixed curve.

How stiff the ice is: stiffer ice sheets stand thicker and hold more sea water. A plastic-ice profile fits Antarctica at about 32 kPa and Greenland at about 80 kPa; the default 50 kPa lies between them and was chosen to meet the model's ice-volume and sea-level targets.
How often granite bodies intrude under volcanic arcs. More plutons mean more granite outcrops and more porphyry host rock.
Typical length of a granite body. Each pluton stands for a whole intrusive suite; larger ones make bigger outcrops.

How far rock layers are evened out sideways, in simulation cells (16 blocks each at the standard scale). Higher values make layers run flatter, with gentler dips; 0 draws each cell's own layers. The default, 10, gives the gentle dips of undisturbed basins; folds and faults are added on top.

Where one rock turns into another along a layer (sandstone into shale, say), the two interlock in tongues instead of meeting at a wall. This sets how thick the tongues are: below 1 finer, above 1 coarser. 1 is the default.
A rock that makes up less than this share of a layer at a spot is left out of the tongues, so a trace of it does not scatter single-block specks. 0 keeps every trace; the default is 0.15.
How big folds and faults are drawn in blocks: every wavelength, length, amplitude and slip is multiplied by it, and fewer of them form so that they cover the same ground.
The typical distance from one anticline to the next (16 km is 53 blocks at the standard scale; the Zagros folds are about 16 km apart).
How far the tightest folds have shortened the rock, as a fraction, in the core of a collision. 0.3 gives limbs dipping about 45°; forelands fold more gently.
How often a train of folds starts in crust that is being shortened.
The typical length of a fault's trace (40 km is 133 blocks at the standard scale). Longer faults slip further.
How far from a fault the rock on its moving side is displaced, as a share of the fault's length: the width of the tilted block.

How far a thrust carries its upper block, as a share of its length (0.08: a 133-block thrust moves rock up to about 11 blocks up its ramp, at full strength and full shortening, less where the rock has shortened less).
How far a normal fault drops its upper block, as a share of its length (0.05: a 133-block fault drops rock about 7 blocks).
How far a strike-slip fault moves rock sideways, as a share of its length.
How often a thrust starts in crust that is being shortened.
How often a normal fault starts in a continental rift.
How often a strike-slip fault starts along a margin where the plates converge obliquely.
How far out from an active mountain belt the crust still folds and thrusts, in km at Earth's size (250 km, the width of the Zagros fold belt, is about 100 blocks on a 16,384-block planet).
How many folds, or faults of one kind, may lie over one another at a place. More makes belts busier where strain lasts long.
How long a fault scarp or fold ridge stays on the ground after the structure formed. Older structures keep their offset in the rock and none at the surface.
How much erosion or burial wipes a structure's relief off the ground, as a multiple of its own height (an active fault renews its scarp, so more than once).
The share of a young fold's amplitude that stands as ridges and valleys.
How far the ground on the still side of a fault moves the other way, as a share of the moving side: the raised shoulders of a rift, the trough in front of a thrust.
How often a granite stock rises in a collision belt or a volcanic arc.
The typical radius of a stock (4 km is 13 blocks at the standard scale). Larger granite bodies are the batholiths above.
How often a basalt dyke is injected along a continental rift.
The typical length of a dyke (15 km is 50 blocks at the standard scale). Dykes are about 2 to 5 blocks wide.

How far a new stratovolcano keeps from the cones already standing along its arc. Real arcs have no fixed spacing: their large centres stand on average 27 to 87 km apart, irregularly. The Volcanoes setting divides it.
How strong the arc's magma supply must be (0–1: convergence speed, less on oceanic crust) before stratovolcanoes form on it.
How high a stratovolcano stands above its surroundings on the weakest arcs.

How high a stratovolcano stands above its surroundings on the fastest-converging arcs (Earth's 512 measured stratovolcanoes: median 1.0 km, the tallest 4.6 km; the default is 2 km, and erosion lowers cones below it).

The radius of the tallest stratovolcanoes' base; lower cones are narrower. Steeper cones come from a smaller radius. The default 10 km with the default top height of 2 km keeps the proportions of a real cone, before the flank setting widens it.
The shortest time a stratovolcano stays active before it dies and starts to erode.
The longest time a stratovolcano stays active. Longer lives leave more young cones standing along arcs.
How far a hotspot's last volcano drifts on its plate before a new one forms over the plume: the spacing of volcanoes in an island chain.
How high a shield volcano rises above the sea floor over the weakest plumes.
How high a shield volcano rises above the sea floor over the strongest plumes (Mauna Loa, Hawaii: about 9 km; the default is 6.5 km).
The radius of the largest shield volcanoes' base.
How high the broad volcanic plateau of a hotspot under a continent stands (Yellowstone's plateau: about 0.5 to 0.8 km above the plain beside it).
The radius of a continental hotspot's volcanic plateau.

An extra sinking of dead volcanoes on ocean floor, on top of the bending of the plate under their weight and the cooling of the old sea floor, which the simulation already does. The default 0 leaves it at that; more turns old islands into seamounts sooner.
The most a dead ocean volcano sinks in all.
How often a volcano of sticky, silica-rich magma blows itself apart and collapses into a caldera, and a tall shield opens a small summit caldera. Continental hotspots have their own rate, below.

How often a continental hotspot's volcanic centre collapses into a caldera while it is active (Yellowstone: three caldera-forming eruptions in about 1.5 Myr; the default is about 1 per Myr). A collapse ends the centre; the hotspot starts a new one once the old has drifted away.
The radius of the smallest calderas (Crater Lake's caldera is 8–10 km across, a radius of 4–5 km; the default is 3 km).
The radius of the largest calderas (Long Valley: 8 to 16 km; Yellowstone, a basin 45 by 85 km across: 22 to 43 km; the default is 9 km).
Continental crust at least this thick makes silica-rich magma: arc volcanoes on it are caldera-prone and made of rhyolite and tuff.
How many lava flows a flood-basalt pile holds in the rock record, each capped by a thin tuff bed.
The height of the steps flood-basalt plateaus erode into (0: no steps). 80 m is 4 blocks.
How quickly an active volcano grows toward its full height.
How fast a dead volcano loses its crater and sharp summit to erosion; its cone's shape fades three times slower.

No volcano's summit rises higher than this above the sea at Earth's gravity with the default crust strength (Earth's highest: about 6.9 km). It scales with the crust strength over gravity, like the plateaus: about 18 km at Mars's gravity.

How many small craters form for each large one among craters of 20 km and more: the number of craters wider than D falls as D to minus this power. Earth's record gives 1.8 there; a higher value means more small craters. Below 20 km the record is flatter and the model follows it whatever this is.
The smallest crater simulated. The default 2 km is seven blocks across, the smallest bowl the terrain can show; smaller craters are many times more common and cost time without showing.

The largest crater a run may make. The default 300 km is the upper estimate for the largest structure known on Earth (Vredefort; estimates run from 150 to 300 km); larger impacts would melt and resurface much of a small planet, which is not simulated.
How fast impactors strike. Asteroids hit Earth at 12 to 20 km/s (about 18 on average); a faster impactor of the same size digs a wider crater and melts more rock.

The density of the impactors: 2,000 to 3,000 kg/m³ for stony asteroids, about 8,000 for iron ones and 500 to 1,500 for comets. The crater sizes follow the setting above; this sets how big the body behind each crater is.

How far from a crater's centre its blanket of ejecta is drawn, in crater radii. The blanket thins with the cube of the distance (1/27 of its rim thickness at 3 radii) and is faded to nothing over its outer 30 %, so none is drawn beyond this reach.

A sea deeper than this many times the impactor's width stops it before the sea floor, so no crater forms (8 in the ocean-impact models of Davison and Collins 2007); shallower water makes a smaller crater, and a body that would dig a large crater on land leaves only a scoured, crater-less patch in water deeper than 3.5 widths. In a 4 km ocean only bodies wider than about a kilometre crater the sea floor.

How fast soil creep rounds a crater's rim and fills its bowl, on top of the erosion and sediment of the land around it. The default 0.01 is an unsourced estimate; at it a 2-km crater fades in about ten million years and a 20-km one in about a billion.
Scales how fast craters fade: the erosion and burial by the land around them and the soil creep above. 0 keeps every crater as fresh as the day it formed; 2 wears them twice as fast.
How wide an ore province is. Small provinces scatter ore types across the map, large ones give each region a single specialty.

How far underground brines flow from mountains and basins. It decides how far from a mountain belt lead–zinc deposits of the Mississippi Valley type can form; longer reach gives them more land to form on.

Banded iron formation inherited in the old interiors of continents, for runs that start after Earth's great age of iron formations (2.6 to 1.85 billion years ago). 0 is none. At 1 every stable continental interior can hold it, which makes iron very common (412 sites on a quick 16k planet over 1,000 Myr).

Vanilla treats land differently near the coast, further in and deep inside a continent (its mountain biomes keep away from the shore). This is how far from the sea the mid-inland zone begins; a smaller number narrows the coastal plain. The default is 200.
How far from the sea the far-inland zone begins, the deep interior of a continent. A smaller number brings interior biomes closer to the coast. The default is 1,000.

The distance from the sea at which land counts as the very middle of a continent. Few worlds have land this far from any coast; lower it to give smaller continents an interior. The default is 5,000. Values above about 8,000 never apply on a 16,384-block planet, whose poles are 8,192 blocks apart.

How wet the climate must be before lowland can turn to swamp, on vanilla's humidity scale (0 driest, 5 wettest); swamps reach full strength 1.5 bands above it, so above 3.5 they cannot reach full strength. Lower lets swamps form in drier climates. The default is 2.5, the middle band.
Swamps only form on the flattest share of the land, ranked by how much the ground rises and falls around it. 0.35 (the default) means the flattest 35 %; higher lets swamps climb onto rougher ground.
How high above the sea a swamp can form: lowland fades out as it approaches this height. The default is 150 m; raise it to allow swamps on high plateaus.

The smallest geologic province (shield, platform, orogen, basin, volcanic plateau, thinned crust, sea floor), in square kilometres. A biome mod that adds regions through TerraBlender, such as Biomes O' Plenty, gives each province one region, so this sets how big its patches are; smaller values mean more, smaller regions. The default is 50,000 km², a small country.

How long after a continental collision its crust still counts as a mountain-belt province (the Appalachians and Urals are old collision belts). The simulated planet collides continents about twice as often as the Earth did, so shorter times make fewer, smaller mountain provinces. The default is 500 Myr.
How long a mountain range raised by an ocean plate sliding under a continent (the Andes) counts as a mountain-belt province after it was lifted. The default is 50 Myr.
How high such a range must stand above the sea to count as a mountain-belt province; lower ground behind a subduction zone stays shield, platform or basin. The default is 1,500 m.
How much water a stream must carry before it is drawn. Lower gives many more small streams; the default is 2 m³/s, a brook a block wide.
The smallest catchment a stream may drain, so very wet hills do not sprout a stream in every gully. The default is 50 km².
Channel width per square root of discharge (hydraulic geometry: width grows with the square root of the flow). The default 1 makes a 100 m³/s river 10 blocks (3 km) wide.
Channel depth per discharge to the power 0.4. The default 0.5 makes a 100 m³/s river about 3 blocks (60 m) deep; every channel holds at least one block of water.
The widest a river may get. The default is 64 blocks.
The deepest a river channel may get. The default is 12 blocks.
How far below the valley floor a river's water sits. The default is 1 block; 0 puts rivers level with their banks, higher values sink them into little gorges.
How much river courses are smoothed, so they curve instead of zig-zagging along the simulation grid. The default is 8 blocks; 0 follows the grid exactly.
The smallest basin that fills with a lake. The default is 1 km², a pond about 10 × 10 blocks.
The shallowest basin, at its deepest point, that fills with a lake. The default is 1 block.
Whether lakes lose water to evaporation, so a lake in a dry climate passes on less, or nothing, to the river leaving it. On by default. Off, every basin fills.

Whether a lake's level follows its water balance: the level where the inflow from its catchment equals the evaporation from its surface. On (the default), a basin in a dry climate holds a lake below its rim, a salt flat or nothing, and only basins that gain water fill and spill. Off, every basin is full to its rim whatever the climate.

How much the land could evaporate in a year per °C of the year's mean temperature above freezing (Holdridge's rule: 58.93 mm a year per °C of biotemperature). It decides how much of the rain runs off into rivers and how fast lakes evaporate. The default is 60; higher makes every climate drier, with smaller rivers and lakes.

What a lake loses in a year at the freezing point: the evaporation of the cool season and the sublimation of its ice. On top of it a lake loses 60 mm a year per °C of the months above freezing. The default 200 gives a cold lake about 600 mm a year (Earth's lakes average about 650) and a tropical one about 2,000; higher shrinks the lakes of cold dry climates.
Scales how much open water evaporates. The default is 1; higher shrinks the lakes of dry climates and turns more basins into salt flats, lower fills more of them.

How much snow a day melts per °C above freezing. Where the summer is too short and cool to melt the year's snow, the rest stays as snow and ice and feeds no river or lake, so ground that never thaws is dry. The default is 4; real snow melts 3 to 8.

A lake is frozen where the mean annual temperature is below this: the maps draw lake ice, and the game ices the lake's surface there and keeps other lakes open, whatever the biome. The default is 0 °C.
How thick the salt crust is on the floor of a basin too dry to hold a lake (a salt flat). The default is 2 blocks of the halite rock; 0 leaves the ground as it is.
Channels at least this wide become river biomes. The default is 6 blocks, so brooks keep the biome of the land around them.
How far beyond a channel's edge its banks are shaped into a slope up from the water. The default is 1 block, plus the share of the channel's half-width below.
The share of a channel's half-width added to its bank zone, so big rivers get wider, gentler banks. The default is 0.5.

Whether caves and canyons leave lake and river water alone. On, they still cut the ground beneath it and may open into a lake or river bed, but never leave air pockets in the water or a hole in a lake's surface. Off, they cut through the water as they do through any other block. On by default.

Caves and any other open space less than this far above the bottom of the world are filled with lava. The default is 10 blocks, the same as in a vanilla world, so with the world's floor at y -352 the lava stands up to y -342. Under a sea bed that deep the lava stays 8 blocks below the bed. 0 means no lava floor.

Cave lakes may be lava instead of water only this close to the bottom of the world; higher lakes are always water. The default is 54 blocks, the same as in a vanilla world, which keeps lava lakes below about y -290. Lake levels come in 40-block steps, so small changes may do nothing. 0 means no lava lakes.

How far under an active volcano's crater the top of its magma chamber lies. The default is 3 km, which is 150 blocks at 20 m per block. Real ones sit about 1 to 9 km down (Kīlauea's at 1 to 4 km; under arc volcanoes about 6 km on average). A chamber that would reach the lava floor is raised.

Scales the magma chamber under every active volcano. At 1 a chamber's radius is a tenth of its volcano's, kept between 1.2 and 4.5 km. 0 means no magma under volcanoes at all: no chambers, no conduits and no crater lava lakes.

The share of active volcanoes on land whose crater holds a lava lake, the most active first. The default is 0.25, one in four. The others have a plug of magma blocks in the crater instead. Volcanoes under the sea never have a lava lake.

Whether the random lava lakes and lava springs that vanilla and the pack scatter through every biome are left out, so lava is found only at active volcanoes and at the bottom of the world. On by default. Off, they generate as in any other world.

How many geothermal fields each active volcano gets, as a multiple of the built-in rule: at 1 a small, quiet volcano gets none or one and a large, active one six or seven. A field is a few hot-spring pools with terraces, or a few fumaroles with sulfur and bleached ground. Nothing is placed in water, under ice or beside a crater's lava. 0 means no geothermal features anywhere.

How far from a volcano's summit its fields may lie, in basal radii. At the default 1 the first field lies within 0.08–0.35 radii of the summit and the others 0.25–1 radius out, on the volcano itself. These distances are multiplied by this setting, so above 1 fields lie beyond the foot, and at 3 even the first can be a radius out. Fields nearer than 0.35 radii to the summit are always fumaroles.

Scales every geothermal feature: a pool's radius, the terrace around it, a fumarole's field of altered ground. At the default the main pool of a hot-spring field has a radius of 2 to 5 blocks (4 to 10 across) and the smaller ones 2 to 3.

A field away from the summit is hot springs only where the year's rain reaches this much and the mean temperature is at least 3 °C; drier or colder ground gets fumaroles and bare altered ground instead. The default is 400 mm, a game setting. 0 puts springs wherever it is warm enough.
